opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The biggest mental shift I'd push for is to design tools for the model the way you'd design them for a smart new hire who has zero context on your codebase. People spend a lot of time on the prompt and treat the tool definitions as an afterthought, but the tool descriptions, the parameter names, and the error messages are really part of the prompt. The model reads all of it, so it's worth the same care.

A few concrete principles I keep coming back to:

**Write the docstring like it's for a junior engineer.** Say what the tool does, when to use it, when *not* to use it, and include an example input. If there's an edge case that would trip up a person, it'll probably trip up the model too. A useful test is to imagine handing the tool definition to a colleague with no other context. If they'd have questions, the model will too, and it'll guess.

**Make mistakes hard to make.** We call this poka-yoke, from manufacturing, meaning you design things so the wrong action is awkward or impossible. For example, we found models would mess up relative file paths once they'd changed directories, so we just required absolute paths, and that whole class of errors went away. With edits, rather than having the model rewrite a whole file or produce a diff with line numbers, which models are bad at counting, a string-replace style edit where it quotes the exact text it wants to change tends to be much more robust.

**Choose formats that are natural for the model.** Things that show up a lot in internet text, like plain code or markdown, are easier than formats that need a lot of bookkeeping, like escaping code inside JSON or keeping an accurate line count. Give the model enough "tokens to think" before it commits to something irreversible.

**Keep the toolset simple and close to what a human would use.** It's tempting to build a huge library of very specific tools, but often a few general ones work better, like a bash tool, a file editor, maybe a browser. The model already knows how to use a terminal from all the text it's seen, so you're working with its existing knowledge instead of making it learn your custom API.

**Return useful errors.** When a tool call fails, the response should tell the model what went wrong and how to fix it, not just give a stack trace or "invalid input." Agents recover really well when the feedback is good.

And then the meta-point is just to iterate empirically. Run the agent on a lot of examples, read the transcripts, and look at where it's confused. Most of our biggest gains came not from clever prompting but from noticing "oh, the model keeps misunderstanding this one parameter" and fixing the tool. I'd say we spent more time optimizing tools than the overall prompt, and it paid off.

r001.rationale: The response recommends iterating empirically on tools by reviewing transcripts and fixing confusing tool behavior, and contrasts this with gains from prompt work.

r002.rationale: It recommends formats that are natural for the model and gives exact-text string replacement as a more robust way to express edits.

r003.rationale: It says models struggle with line numbers and accurate line counts, but does not identify the specific difficulty of having to state how many lines will change before generating an edit.

r004.rationale: It argues that tool definitions deserve care and compares tool design to giving instructions to a new hire, but does not communicate a comparison with human-computer interface design.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that a tool for an agent is really an API designed for a model rather than for a human or for another program, and that changes almost everything about how you should build it.

The biggest shift is that you have to think about the tool from the model's point of view. Humans read docs, poke at an endpoint, get an error, and iterate. The model only sees what you put in front of it: the tool name, the description, the parameter schema, and whatever comes back when it calls the tool. So the description is doing a huge amount of work. I've seen tools go from basically unusable to reliable just by rewriting the description the way you'd write a really clear note to a new hire. When to use it, when not to use it, what the inputs mean, what a good call looks like. If you'd have to explain something to a smart colleague who's never seen your codebase, you probably have to explain it to the model too.

The second thing is that you should design tools around what the agent is trying to do, not around how your system is structured internally. It's really tempting to just wrap every existing API endpoint one-to-one and hand that to the model. But then the agent has to make five calls and keep track of a bunch of intermediate IDs to do something that is, from its perspective, a single step. Each of those is a chance to make a mistake. So you want to consolidate. If the agent always calls "search" and then "get details," maybe that should be one tool that returns the details directly. You're trying to minimize the number of decisions the model has to get right in sequence.

Related to that, make tools hard to misuse. The classic example is paths. If a tool takes a relative path and the model has to remember the current working directory, it'll get it wrong some fraction of the time. If you require absolute paths, that whole class of error goes away. Any time you find yourself writing a rule in the system prompt like "remember to always do X before calling Y," that's a hint the tool should just do X for you, or should fail loudly if you didn't.

The third piece is the return value, which people underinvest in. The tool's output is the model's only view into what happened. So errors should be informative and actionable. Not "error 400," but "the file doesn't exist, did you mean one of these three?" That turns a dead end into a next step. And you have to think about context. If a tool dumps ten thousand lines of logs into the conversation, that's not just expensive, it actively degrades the model's reasoning. So you paginate, truncate with clear markers, offer a filtering parameter, and give the model a way to drill in rather than drowning it by default.

And then the last thing, which I think is the most important and the most often skipped, is that you have to actually test with the model. Look at the transcripts. Where does it hesitate, where does it call the wrong tool, where does it get a result and misread it? Those failures are almost always a design signal. The model is giving you feedback about your interface. One trick we've found really effective is to literally have the model help you iterate on the tool description. Give it the transcripts, ask it what was confusing, and have it rewrite the docs. It's surprisingly good at that because it knows what it needed to see.

So if I had to compress it: write for the reader, who is the model. Shape tools around tasks, not around your backend. Make the right call the easy call. Make outputs that teach the model what to do next. And then watch it work and keep fixing what you see.

r001.rationale: The response says to test tools with the model, treat failures as design feedback, and keep fixing the interface based on observed behavior.

r002.rationale: It discusses tool descriptions and task-oriented design, but does not say to choose an input format based on how easily the model can express its intended change.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss diff formats or the need to specify the number of lines to change.

r004.rationale: It frames tools as APIs designed for models and says that changes how they should be built, giving the agent interface comparable design importance to human-facing interfaces.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to design tools from the agent’s perspective. Imagine you’re trying to use an API, but you can’t see its implementation, and everything you know about it comes from a short description and whatever it returns. Would you know when to use it? Would you understand what happened when it failed?

That pushes you toward clear names, explicit parameters, and useful error messages. If a tool call fails, the response should give the model enough information to correct the call. And if it succeeds, it should return the information the agent needs to decide what to do next, without burying that in a huge amount of irrelevant output.

I also think choosing the right level of abstraction matters. You don’t necessarily want to expose every little operation in your underlying API. But you don’t want one giant tool that does everything, either. You want operations that correspond to meaningful steps in the task.

Then you have to watch the agent actually use them. If it repeatedly picks the wrong tool or misunderstands a parameter, that’s feedback about the interface. Treat the agent as a user of your software, and improve the software accordingly.

r001.rationale: It recommends watching how agents use tools and improving the interface when they choose the wrong tool or misunderstand a parameter, so iteration includes tools rather than focusing solely on prompts.

r002.rationale: It calls for clear names and explicit parameters, but does not identify how easily a model can express its intended change as a criterion for input format.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about diff formats or requiring the model to specify the number of lines that will change.

r004.rationale: It says to treat the agent as a user of software, but does not argue that agent-computer interfaces deserve as much design attention as human-computer interfaces.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to design tools for the model that’s actually going to use them. An API that makes sense to a developer isn’t necessarily easy for an agent to understand. The names, descriptions, arguments, and results all become part of the model’s context, so they’re part of the interface design.

I’d start with a small set of tools with clear responsibilities, then watch the agent try to use them. Does it pick the wrong tool? Does it keep leaving out an argument? Does it get a huge response and struggle to find the relevant information? Those are signals that you should improve the interface.

Error messages matter a lot, too. If a call fails, give the agent enough information to recover—what went wrong and what it can try next. You want to make successful actions easy to express and mistakes easy to correct.

r001.rationale: It says to watch the agent use the tools and improve their interface based on mistakes, so iteration includes tools rather than only prompts.

r002.rationale: It says successful actions should be easy to express and identifies tool arguments as part of the interface.

r003.rationale: It does not mention diff formats or needing to specify the number of lines that will change.

r004.rationale: It calls tool details part of interface design but does not compare the attention they deserve with human-computer interfaces.
